theorems.name: Normality from the minimal polynomials of generators
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be algebraic and suppose a family $(a_i)$ generates $E$ over $F$.
theorems.statement: The extension is normal exactly when the minimal polynomial over $F$ of each $a_i$ splits over $E$.
theorems.proof: If every generating polynomial splits, every embedding into an algebraic closure carries the field into itself. The same finite-root permutation argument as for an algebraic endomorphism gives equality of images.

theorems.subject: field-tower
theorems.name: Restriction and extension of automorphisms in normal towers
theorems.hypotheses: Let $F\subseteq E\subseteq L$ be a tower of algebraic field extensions.
theorems.statement: If $E/F$ is normal, every $F$-automorphism of $L$ preserves $E$. If $L/F$ is normal, every $F$-embedding $E\to L$ extends to an $F$-automorphism of $L$.
theorems.proof: Normality of $E/F$ fixes the image of $E$ under any embedding. For extension, enlarge the embedding into an algebraic closure using the algebraic embedding theorem. Normality of $L/F$ then makes its image equal to $L$.

theorems.subject: field-map
theorems.name: Embeddings of a normal extension differ by an automorphism
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be algebraic normal and let $L/F$ be a field extension admitting an $F$-embedding $u:E\to L$.
theorems.statement: Every $F$-embedding $v:E\to L$ has the unique form $u\circ\sigma$ with $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}_F(E)$.
theorems.proof: The images of $u$ and $v$ coincide because both contain precisely all conjugates of elements of $E$ under the generating description. Set $\sigma=u^{-1}v$.

theorems.subject: field-polynomial
theorems.name: Existence and normality of splitting fields
theorems.hypotheses: Let $P\in F[T]$ be nonconstant over a field $F$.
theorems.statement: The subfield of an algebraic closure generated by all roots of $P$ is a finite normal extension of $F$, unique up to $F$-isomorphism. Every extension in which $P$ splits contains an $F$-isomorphic copy of it.
theorems.proof: There are finitely many algebraic roots. Embeddings permute the roots, which yields normality. Successively choosing corresponding roots yields a map to any field in which the polynomial splits.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Finite normal closures
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite and view $E$ inside an algebraic closure of $F$.
theorems.statement: There is a least intermediate field containing $E$ and normal over $F$. It is finite over $F$, and it is Galois over $F$ when $E/F$ is separable.
theorems.proof: Take the splitting field of the product of the minimal polynomials of finitely many generators. Every normal field containing the generators contains their conjugates. In the separable case every adjoined root is separable.
refs: Stacks 0EXM · normal closure of a finite separable extension

theorems.subject: field-tower
theorems.name: Finite normal subextensions inside a normal extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $L/F$ be algebraic normal and $E$ an intermediate field.
theorems.statement: If $E/F$ is finite, its normal closure over $F$ lies in $L$ and is finite. If $E/F$ is normal and $M/E$ is a finite intermediate extension in $L$, then $M$ is contained in an intermediate field normal over $F$ and finite over $E$.
theorems.proof: For the first statement all roots required by the normal closure already lie in $L$. For the second, choose a finite set of generators of $M/E$ and adjoin all their conjugates over $F$ to $E$.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Normal closure as a quotient of a tensor product
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite and let $N$ be its normal closure in an algebraic closure of $F$.
theorems.statement: The tensor product over $F$ of $[E:F]_s$ copies of $E$ has a surjective $F$-algebra map onto $N$.
theorems.proof: Index the tensor factors by the embeddings of $E$ into the algebraic closure. Their images generate the normal closure. The subalgebra they generate is a field because it is an intermediate subring of an algebraic extension.
refs: Stacks 0BID · algebraic intermediate subrings are fields

theorems.subject: field
theorems.name: Finite subgroups of the multiplicative group are cyclic
theorems.hypotheses: Let $H$ be a finite subgroup of $F^\times$ for a field $F$.
theorems.statement: The group $H$ is cyclic. For each positive integer $n$, the subgroup of $n$th roots of unity is cyclic of order dividing $n$.
theorems.proof: If $n$ is an exponent of the group, for each $d$ dividing $n$ the elements of order dividing $d$ are roots of $T^d-1$ and number at most $d$. The cyclicity criterion for abelian groups applies.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Characteristic polynomial, trace and norm from a minimal polynomial
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite, and let $a\in E$ have monic minimal polynomial $P(T)=T^d+c_1T^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d$. Put $m=[E:F(a)]$.
theorems.statement: The characteristic polynomial of multiplication by $a$ is $P(T)^m$. Consequently $\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F}(a)=-mc_1$ and $\operatorname{N}_{E/F}(a)=(-1)^{[E:F]}c_d^m$.
theorems.proof: Choose an $F(a)$-basis of $E$. On each of the resulting summands the multiplication operator has characteristic polynomial $P$. Compare the leading and constant coefficients.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Trace and determinant under restriction of scalars
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite, $V$ a finite-dimensional $E$-vector space, and $u$ an $E$-linear endomorphism.
theorems.statement: $\operatorname{Tr}_F(u)=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F}(\operatorname{Tr}_E(u))$ and $\det_F(u)=\operatorname{N}_{E/F}(\det_E(u))$.
theorems.proof: The trace follows by writing the $E$-matrix entries as multiplication operators on the $F$-vector space $E$. For the determinant, check elementary matrices and diagonal matrices in the invertible case. A singular map has zero determinant over both fields.

theorems.subject: field-tower
theorems.name: Transitivity of trace and norm
theorems.hypotheses: Let $F\subseteq E\subseteq L$ be a tower of finite field extensions.
theorems.statement: $\operatorname{Tr}_{L/F}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{L/E}$ and $\operatorname{N}_{L/F}=\operatorname{N}_{E/F}\circ\operatorname{N}_{L/E}$.
theorems.proof: Apply restriction of scalars to the $E$-linear map on $L$ given by multiplication by each element of $L$.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Discriminant of a quadratic field extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ have degree $2$ and let $u\in E\setminus F$ have minimal polynomial $T^2+bT+c$.
theorems.statement: The discriminant in the basis $(1,u)$ is $b^2-4c$. In characteristic $2$ it is zero in the purely inseparable case and has trivial nonzero square class in the separable case. In characteristic different from $2$ it is a nonsquare and adjoining its square root gives $E$.
theorems.proof: Use the multiplication matrices for $1$, $u$ and $u^2$ to compute the trace-pairing determinant. In characteristic $2$ the derivative is $b$, while in other characteristics the identity $(2u+b)^2=b^2-4c$ gives the quadratic description.
refs: Stacks 0BIL · separability and the trace pairing

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: A faithful finite group action yields a Galois extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let a finite group $G$ act faithfully by field automorphisms on a field $E$.
theorems.statement: For the fixed field $F=E^G$, the extension $E/F$ is finite Galois with degree $|G|$, and the given action identifies $G$ with $\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$.
theorems.proof: The polynomial attached to each finite orbit has coefficients in $F$ and distinct roots. The field degree is bounded by $|G|$ using these orbit polynomials and the primitive element theorem on finite subextensions. Independence of distinct automorphisms gives the opposite bound.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Finite Galois correspondence
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite Galois with group $G$.
theorems.statement: The assignments $H\mapsto E^H$ and $M\mapsto\operatorname{Gal}(E/M)$ are inverse inclusion-reversing bijections between subgroups and intermediate fields. Normal subgroups correspond to intermediate extensions Galois over $F$.
theorems.proof: Apply the fixed-field theorem to each subgroup. Over any intermediate field the extension is Galois, so that intermediate field is the fixed field of its automorphism group. Conjugation transports fixed fields and detects normality.
refs: Stacks 09I2 · Galois extensions over intermediate fields

theorems.subject: field-tower
theorems.name: Galois restriction exact sequence
theorems.hypotheses: Let $F\subseteq E\subseteq L$ with $L/F$ and $E/F$ Galois, finite or infinite.
theorems.statement: Restriction gives $1\to\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)\to\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\to1$. With Krull topologies these are continuous maps and the sequence is exact as profinite groups.
theorems.proof: The kernel consists of the automorphisms fixing $E$. An $F$-automorphism of $E$ extends to $L$ by normality. Continuity is checked on the stabilizers of finite subsets.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Galois groups are profinite in the Krull topology
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be Galois. Give $E$ the discrete topology and $G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$ the topology of pointwise convergence.
theorems.statement: The group $G$ is the inverse limit of the finite Galois groups of the finite Galois subextensions of $E/F$, with surjective restriction maps. Its underlying space is profinite.
theorems.proof: Finite Galois subextensions are directed under inclusion and exhaust $E$. Compatible automorphisms on them give a unique automorphism of $E$. Finite-subextension restriction determines the topology.
refs: Stacks 0BU2 · inverse limit over finite Galois subextensions

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Infinite Galois correspondence
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be Galois with Krull-topological group $G$.
theorems.statement: Closed subgroups of $G$ and intermediate fields correspond contravariantly by fixed field and pointwise stabilizer. Open subgroups correspond to finite subextensions, and closed normal subgroups to Galois subextensions.
theorems.proof: Apply the finite Galois correspondence to the finite Galois subextensions. A subgroup is recovered from its finite restriction images precisely when it is closed.

theorems.subject: field
theorems.name: Algebraic closedness of the complex numbers
theorems.hypotheses: Let the field be $\mathbf C$.
theorems.statement: Every nonconstant polynomial over $\mathbf C$ has a root, and $\mathbf C$ is algebraically closed.
theorems.proof: If a nonconstant polynomial has no zero, its reciprocal is bounded and entire, contradicting Liouville’s theorem.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Kummer generator for a cyclic Galois extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be cyclic Galois of degree $n$. Assume that the characteristic of $F$ does not divide $n$, and that $F$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity.
theorems.statement: There is an element $z\in E$ with $E=F(z)$ and $z^n\in F$.
theorems.proof: The linear operator given by a generator of the cyclic group has an eigenvector for a primitive $n$th root of unity by the character projection and independence of automorphisms. The vector has an orbit of size $n$, and its $n$th power is fixed.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Adjoining a primitive root of unity of prime order
theorems.hypotheses: Let $p$ be prime, $\operatorname{char}(F)\ne p$, and $\zeta$ a primitive $p$th root of unity in an algebraic closure.
theorems.statement: $F(\zeta)/F$ is Galois, with degree dividing $p-1$.
theorems.proof: It splits $T^p-1$, which has distinct roots, and its Galois group embeds in $(\mathbf Z/p\mathbf Z)^\times$ by its faithful action on $\zeta$.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Intermediate fields in a radical extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E=F(a)$ have degree $e$ over $F$, with $a^e\in F$. Assume every $e$th root of unity in $E$ belongs to $F$.
theorems.statement: Each intermediate field is $F(a^d)$ for some divisor $d$ of $e$.
theorems.proof: Use the source result on radical extensions. Its root-of-unity hypothesis and the equality between the exponent and the field degree are both required here.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Artin–Schreier generator for a cyclic degree-p extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$ and let $E/F$ be cyclic Galois of degree $p$.
theorems.statement: There is an element $z\in E$ with $E=F(z)$ and $z^p-z\in F$.
theorems.proof: For a generator $\sigma$ of the Galois group, the $F$-linear operator $\sigma-1$ has image equal to the trace-zero subspace. As $1$ has trace zero, choose $z$ with $\sigma(z)-z=1$. This gives the full orbit and makes $z^p-z$ invariant.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Existence and size of transcendence bases
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be any field extension.
theorems.statement: Transcendence bases exist and all have the same cardinality.
theorems.proof: Take a maximal algebraically independent family by Zorn’s lemma. Exchange of algebraically independent elements gives invariance of cardinality.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Transcendence degree of fields generated by special real numbers
theorems.hypotheses: Use the real numbers $e$ and $\pi$ over $\mathbf Q$.
theorems.statement: The field $\mathbf Q(\pi)$ is purely transcendental of transcendence degree one. The transcendence degree of $\mathbf Q(e,\pi)$ is at least one and at most two.
theorems.proof: The transcendence of $\pi$ makes it a single algebraically independent generator. For the second field, the two generators bound the transcendence degree above, and its subfield $\mathbf Q(\pi)$ gives the lower bound.

theorems.subject: field-family
theorems.name: Distinct transcendence bases of the same field extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $T$ be an indeterminate over $F$ and take the extension $F(T)/F$.
theorems.statement: Both $(T)$ and $(T^2)$ are transcendence bases of the same field extension.
theorems.proof: Both elements are transcendental, and $T$ is algebraic over $F(T^2)$ because it is a root of $X^2-T^2$. This argument also applies in characteristic two.

theorems.subject: field-tower
theorems.name: Transcendence degree in a tower
theorems.hypotheses: Let $F\subseteq E\subseteq L$ be a tower of field extensions.
theorems.statement: $\operatorname{trdeg}_F L=\operatorname{trdeg}_F E+\operatorname{trdeg}_E L$, using cardinal addition.
theorems.proof: The union of a transcendence basis of $E/F$ and a transcendence basis of $L/E$ is a transcendence basis of $L/F$.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Adjoining indeterminates preserves finite extension degree
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be finite and $x_1,\dots,x_r$ algebraically independent over $E$.
theorems.statement: $[E(x_1,\dots,x_r):F(x_1,\dots,x_r)]=[E:F]$.
theorems.proof: An $F$-basis of $E$ remains linearly independent over the rational function field of $F$ by clearing denominators and comparing coefficients. It spans the resulting finite field extension.

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Relative algebraic closure in a finitely generated extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be a finitely generated field extension.
theorems.statement: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in $E$ is finite over $F$.
theorems.proof: Choose a finite transcendence basis $S$ of $E/F$. Every finite subextension of the relative algebraic closure has degree over $F$ at most $[E:F(S)]$ by adjoining $S$ and using the tower law. The bounded degrees force the relative algebraic closure to be finite.
refs: Stacks 0G1M · degree unchanged by adjoining indeterminates

theorems.subject: field-extension
theorems.name: Tensor product decomposition of a normal algebraic extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be algebraic normal. Let $E_s$ and $E_i$ be the subfields of separable and purely inseparable elements over $F$.
theorems.statement: The extension $E_s/F$ is Galois and $E/E_s$ purely inseparable. The extension $E_i/F$ is purely inseparable and $E/E_i$ Galois. Multiplication identifies $E_s\otimes_F E_i$ with $E$.
theorems.proof: The separable part is the canonical separable subextension. In a normal extension the purely inseparable part is fixed by all base-field automorphisms. The source result gives the two factorizations and linear disjointness.
refs: Stacks 0EXK · normality of the separable part

theorems.subject: field-element
theorems.name: A pth-root test in a separable algebraic extension
theorems.hypotheses: Let $E/F$ be separable algebraic in characteristic $p>0$ and let $a\in E$. Assume $a$ is a root of a polynomial $P\in F[T]$ with distinct roots in an algebraic closure and coefficients in $F^p$.
theorems.statement: The element $a$ is a $p$th power in $E$. This applies in particular if its minimal polynomial over $F$ has all coefficients in $F^p$.
theorems.proof: Take $p$th roots of the coefficients of $P$ to obtain a polynomial $Q$ with distinct roots. A $p$th root of $a$ is a root of $Q$. If it were absent from $E$, the irreducible polynomial $T^p-a$ over $E$ would divide $Q$, contradicting distinct roots.
refs: Stacks 09HF · irreducibility of a missing pth-root polynomial

theorems.subject: ring-ideal-pair
theorems.name: Henselian local rings and pairs
theorems.hypotheses: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a local ring with its unique maximal ideal.
theorems.statement: The local ring is henselian if and only if the pair $(A,\mathfrak m)$ is henselian.
theorems.proof: The local ring is henselian if and only if the pair $(A,\mathfrak m)$ is henselian.

theorems.subject: ring-ideal-pair
theorems.name: Finite étale algebras over a henselian pair
theorems.hypotheses: Let $(A,I)$ be a henselian pair.
theorems.statement: Base change $B\mapsto B/IB$ gives an equivalence from finite étale $A$-algebras to finite étale $A/I$-algebras.
theorems.proof: Base change $B\mapsto B/IB$ gives an equivalence from finite étale $A$-algebras to finite étale $A/I$-algebras.

theorems.subject: ring-ideal-pair
theorems.name: Radical invariance of the henselian pair property
theorems.hypotheses: Let $I,J$ be ideals of $A$ with $\sqrt I=\sqrt J$.
theorems.statement: The pair $(A,I)$ is henselian if and only if $(A,J)$ is henselian.
theorems.proof: The pair $(A,I)$ is henselian if and only if $(A,J)$ is henselian.

theorems.subject: ring-ideal-pair
theorems.name: Henselianity along a chain of ideals
theorems.hypotheses: Let $I\subseteq J$ be ideals of a commutative ring $A$.
theorems.statement: The pair $(A,J)$ is henselian if and only if both $(A,I)$ and $(A/I,J/I)$ are henselian.
theorems.proof: The pair $(A,J)$ is henselian if and only if both $(A,I)$ and $(A/I,J/I)$ are henselian.

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Reduced ring and its affine spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: The ring $R$ is reduced if and only if the scheme $X$ is reduced. One direction uses that localizations of reduced rings are reduced; the other tests global sections.
theorems.proof: The ring $R$ is reduced if and only if the scheme $X$ is reduced. One direction uses that localizations of reduced rings are reduced; the other tests global sections.
refs: Stacks 01J2 · reducedness of an affine scheme

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Integral domain and its affine spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $R$ is a domain if and only if $X$ is integral. The nonzero requirement on $R$ corresponds to the nonempty requirement for an irreducible scheme.
theorems.proof: $R$ is a domain if and only if $X$ is integral. The nonzero requirement on $R$ corresponds to the nonempty requirement for an irreducible scheme.

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Noetherian ring and its affine spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $R$ is Noetherian if and only if $X$ is a Noetherian scheme. This tests the ringed space and does not follow from the topology alone.
theorems.proof: $R$ is Noetherian if and only if $X$ is a Noetherian scheme. This tests the ringed space and does not follow from the topology alone.

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Zero dimensionality and a profinite affine spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: The Zariski space of $X$ is profinite exactly when every prime of $R$ is maximal. Indeed the affine scheme is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so its underlying space is spectral; closed points correspond to maximal ideals.
theorems.proof: The Zariski space of $X$ is profinite exactly when every prime of $R$ is maximal. Indeed the affine scheme is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so its underlying space is spectral; closed points correspond to maximal ideals.

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Absolute flatness, reducedness and a profinite spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $R$ is absolutely flat exactly when $R$ is reduced and the Zariski space of $X$ is profinite. Profinite topology alone cannot detect nilpotent elements of the coordinate ring.
theorems.proof: $R$ is absolutely flat exactly when $R$ is reduced and the Zariski space of $X$ is profinite. Profinite topology alone cannot detect nilpotent elements of the coordinate ring.
refs: Stacks 01J3 · reduced closed subscheme on a given closed subset

theorems.subject: ring
theorems.name: Regular ring and its affine spectrum
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and put $X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. Assume that $R$ is Noetherian.
theorems.statement: Regularity of $R$ (each $R_{\mathfrak p}$ regular local) is equivalent to regularity of $X$.
theorems.proof: Regularity of $R$ (each $R_{\mathfrak p}$ regular local) is equivalent to regularity of $X$.

theorems.subject: ring-map
theorems.name: Finite ring map and its affine morphism
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings with identity and put $f=\operatorname{Spec}(A\leftarrow R):\operatorname{Spec}(A)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $A$ is finite as an $R$-module if and only if $f$ is finite.
theorems.proof: $A$ is finite as an $R$-module if and only if $f$ is finite.

theorems.subject: ring-map
theorems.name: Finite type ring map and its affine morphism
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings with identity and put $f=\operatorname{Spec}(A\leftarrow R):\operatorname{Spec}(A)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $A$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra if and only if $f$ is of finite type; the morphism of affine schemes is quasi-compact.
theorems.proof: $A$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra if and only if $f$ is of finite type; the morphism of affine schemes is quasi-compact.
refs: Stacks 01T1 · definition of finite type morphism

theorems.subject: ring-map
theorems.name: Flat ring map and its affine morphism
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings with identity and put $f=\operatorname{Spec}(A\leftarrow R):\operatorname{Spec}(A)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $A$ is flat as an $R$-module if and only if $f$ is flat. Flatness of the morphism is checked on local rings, or equivalently on affine charts.
theorems.proof: $A$ is flat as an $R$-module if and only if $f$ is flat. Flatness of the morphism is checked on local rings, or equivalently on affine charts.

theorems.subject: ring-map
theorems.name: Étale ring map and its affine morphism
theorems.hypotheses: Let $R\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings with identity and put $f=\operatorname{Spec}(A\leftarrow R):\operatorname{Spec}(A)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$.
theorems.statement: $R\to A$ is étale if and only if $f$ is étale. The algebraic property is local on the source and target, and local finite presentation is part of the geometric definition.
theorems.proof: $R\to A$ is étale if and only if $f$ is étale. The algebraic property is local on the source and target, and local finite presentation is part of the geometric definition.

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: The zero ring
examples.proof: It has a single ideal, no prime ideals, and no nonzero nilpotent elements. Its prime-localization conditions are vacuous. It has no proper maximal ideal.

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A product of two fields is normal but not a domain
examples.proof: Prime localization projects onto one factor, so both local rings are fields. The two factor idempotents are nonzero and have product zero. The spectrum has two closed points.

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: Dual numbers are Artinian and nonreduced
examples.proof: For any field k take $k[t]/(t^2)$. It has length two over itself. The class of t is nonzero and has square zero. The only prime is its nonzero maximal ideal, and the regular locus is empty.
refs: Stacks 07P7 · J-1 need not imply J-0

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: The integers are a PID and Jacobson but not a field or local
examples.proof: Every ideal of the integers is generated by its least positive element unless it is zero. Every rational prime generates a distinct maximal ideal. The chains (0) ⊊ (p) show that its dimension is one.

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: The integers localized at 2 form a nonhenselian DVR
examples.proof: In $\mathbf Z_{(2)}$ every nonzero element is a unit times a power of 2. The reduction of $T^2-T-4$ has a simple root at zero. The polynomial has no root in the fraction field because 17 is not a rational square.
refs: Stacks 04GM · complete local rings are henselian

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A two-variable polynomial ring is a UFD but not a PID
examples.proof: For a field k the ring $k[x,y]$ is a UFD by the polynomial-ring theorem. A generator of (x,y) would divide both x and y, so it would be a unit, contrary to (x,y) being proper. The primes (0) ⊊ (x) ⊊ (x,y) give a chain of length two.
refs: Stacks 0BC1 · polynomial ring over a UFD
Stacks 00FO · finite type algebras over a field are Noetherian
Stacks 00G1 · finite type algebras over a field are Jacobson

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A cuspidal domain is not integrally closed
examples.proof: For a field k the subring $k[t^2,t^3]$ of $k[t]$ is a finite type domain. The element t lies in its fraction field as the quotient of its third and second powers and satisfies a monic quadratic with coefficients in the subring. The monomials in the subring have no term of degree one.
refs: Stacks 0309 · integral closure in the fraction field
Stacks 00FO · finite type algebras over a field are Noetherian
Stacks 00G1 · finite type algebras over a field are Jacobson

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A reduced local ring need not be a domain or normal
examples.proof: Localize $k[x,y]/(xy)$ at the ideal (x,y). The ideal (xy) is the intersection of the prime ideals (x) and (y) before localization, hence is radical. Both minimal primes survive localization and have dimension-one quotients. The nonzero images of x and y multiply to zero.

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: An infinite product of fields is absolutely flat but not Noetherian
examples.proof: For a field k consider the countable product of copies of k. The absolute flatness theorem applies. Ideals supported in the first n factors form a strictly increasing chain. A finite product of fields is Artinian and Noetherian.
refs: Stacks 092G · arbitrary products of absolutely flat rings

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A nondiscrete valuation ring need not be Noetherian
examples.proof: Take the union of the local rings $k[t^{1/n!}]_{(t^{1/n!})}$ for n at least 1 with compatible embeddings. The order of t has value group the rationals, and the union is its nonnegative valuation ring. The ideals generated by the displayed uniformizers strictly increase as n increases.
refs: Stacks 0AS4 · filtered colimits of valuation rings

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: A local ring can have one prime and a nonnilpotent nilradical
examples.proof: Take the polynomial ring in countably many variables over a field, modulo the squares of the variables. The ideal of their images is the only prime and the Jacobson radical. Products of arbitrarily many distinct variables survive, so the nilradical is not nilpotent and the ring is not Noetherian.
refs: Stacks 0G62 · Noetherian spectrum of a non-Noetherian ring
Stacks 00IM · nilpotence over a Noetherian ring

examples.subject: ring
examples.name: The rational field is henselian but not strictly henselian
examples.proof: The rational field is local with zero maximal ideal and the simple-root lifting condition holds by reduction along the identity. Its residue field has a proper quadratic separable extension obtained by adjoining a square root of 2.
refs: Stacks 04GF · strict henselianity and simple-root lifting

examples.subject: module
examples.name: The rational numbers as an integer module
examples.proof: $\mathbf Q$ is a localization of $\mathbf Z$, so it is flat and torsion free. Finitely many rational generators have bounded denominators. Every map $\mathbf Q\to\mathbf Z$ vanishes by divisibility. A nonzero projective module is a summand of a free module and therefore has a nonzero coordinate map to $\mathbf Z$. At every maximal ideal the residue fibre of $\mathbf Q$ vanishes.

examples.subject: module
examples.name: A summand with variable rank
examples.proof: For a field $k$ let $R=k\times k$ and $M=(k,0)$. The idempotent $(1,0)$ exhibits $M$ as a direct summand of $R$. Its ranks at the two primes are one and zero, so it cannot be globally free. The zero fibre also precludes faithful flatness.

examples.subject: module
examples.name: A torsion-free ideal that is not flat as a module
examples.proof: In the domain $R=k[x,y]$, the ideal $M=(x,y)$ is torsion free and finitely generated. At $\mathfrak m=(x,y)$ its rank over the fraction field is one, but $M_\mathfrak m/\mathfrak mM_\mathfrak m$ has dimension two over $k$. It is not free over $R_\mathfrak m$. If it were flat there, finite generation over a local ring would make it free.

examples.subject: module
examples.name: Nonzero fibres without flatness
examples.proof: Over $\mathbf Z$ let $M=\mathbf Z\oplus\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z$. The free summand supplies a nonzero fibre at every maximal ideal. Multiplication by two has a nonzero kernel on $M$, so $M$ is not flat over the domain.

examples.subject: module
examples.name: Finite generation does not imply finite length
examples.proof: The module $\mathbf Z$ is free of rank one over itself. The descending sequence $2^n\mathbf Z$ is strictly decreasing, whereas any module of finite length satisfies the descending chain condition on submodules.

examples.subject: module
examples.name: A cyclic module without a finite presentation
examples.proof: Let $V$ be an infinite-dimensional $k$-vector space and $R=k\oplus V$ the square-zero extension, with ideal $I=0\oplus V$. The quotient $M=R/I$ is cyclic. The kernel $I$ of the displayed surjection from $R$ is not finitely generated, as its $R$-module structure factors through $k$. This prevents finite presentation. Also $I\otimes_R M=I/I^2\ne0$ maps to zero in $M$.

examples.subject: ideal
examples.name: A radical ideal that is not prime
examples.proof: In $k[x,y]$, the ideal $(xy)$ equals $(x)\cap(y)$ and is radical. Neither $x$ nor $y$ is in $(xy)$, so the ideal is not prime.

examples.subject: ideal
examples.name: A prime ideal that is not maximal
examples.proof: The zero ideal of $k[t]$ is prime, because the quotient is a domain. The strictly larger ideal $(t)$ is proper.

examples.subject: ideal
examples.name: A locally nilpotent ideal without a uniform exponent
examples.proof: Let $R=k[x_1,x_2,\ldots]/(x_i^2:i\ge1)$ and $I=(x_i:i\ge1)$. Every element of $I$ uses finitely many variables, whose generated ideal has a power equal to zero. For every $n$, the square-free monomial $x_1\cdots x_n$ survives and lies in $I^n$. The classes of all $x_i$ are linearly independent in $I/I^2$ over $R/I=k$, preventing finite generation.

examples.subject: ideal
examples.name: A regular ideal with nonflat quotient
examples.proof: In $R=k[t]$ let $I=(t)$. The element $t$ is a nonzero divisor and generates a prime maximal ideal. Its quotient is not flat because tensoring the injective multiplication-by-$t$ map on $R$ with $R/I$ gives the zero endomorphism of a nonzero module.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: Inverting two in the integers
examples.proof: $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z[1/2]$ is a principal localization. The element $1/2$ is not integral over $\mathbf Z$: multiply a hypothetical monic equation of degree $n$ by $2^n$ to obtain an odd integer equal to zero. The prime $(2)$ has empty fibre, and $1/2$ has no preimage.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: The fraction field of the integers
examples.proof: $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Q$ is a localization. A finite family of rational numbers generates a subalgebra contained in $\mathbf Z[1/d]$ for one nonzero integer $d$. This misses the reciprocal of any prime not dividing $d$. Hence the map is not of finite type.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: Reduction modulo two
examples.proof: $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z$ is a quotient by a principal ideal, so it is finite and G-unramified. Multiplication by two is injective on the source module but becomes zero after tensoring with the target, so the map is not flat.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: Dual numbers over a characteristic zero field
examples.proof: For $k$ a field of characteristic zero, $k\to S=k[t]/(t^2)$ has free target module on $1,t$. Its spectrum maps onto the single point of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, and $t^2$ is a regular sequence of length one in $k[t]$, so the map is syntomic. The differential module $S\,dt/(2t\,dt)$ is nonzero and is not free over the local ring $S$. It cannot be finite projective over $S$.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: The affine line over a field
examples.proof: For any field $k$, $k\to k[t]$ is standard smooth, using an empty family of relations. Its fibre over the unique prime of $k$ is $k[t]$, of infinite dimension over $k$, and $t$ is not integral over $k$.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: Projection onto an idempotent factor
examples.proof: For a field $k$, the projection $k\times k\to k$ identifies with localization at $(1,0)$. The other factor is a nonzero kernel and its point is absent from the image of spectra.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: A finite quotient with infinitely many relations
examples.proof: Let $R=k\oplus V$ with $V$ infinite-dimensional over $k$ and $V^2=0$. The quotient $R\to k$ is finite and unramified. Its kernel cannot be generated by finitely many elements. Finite presentation of the quotient algebra would force finite generation of that kernel. Tensoring the kernel inclusion with $k$ kills the nonzero module $V/V^2$, so the quotient is not flat.

examples.subject: ring-map
examples.name: A reduced algebra acquiring a nilpotent after field extension
examples.proof: Let $p$ be prime, $k=\mathbf F_p(t)$, and $S=k[u]/(u^p-t)$. The polynomial is irreducible since $t$ has valuation one and is not a $p$th power in $k$. Thus $S$ is a field. The algebra $S\otimes_k S$ is $S[v]/((v-u)^p)$ and has a nonzero nilpotent. The finite field extension is inseparable, so the map is not étale.

examples.subject: field
examples.name: The rational number field
examples.proof: The rationals have degree one over their prime subfield and characteristic zero. The polynomial $X^2-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbf Q$ and separable, giving a nontrivial quadratic extension.
refs: Stacks 09FG · source example or supporting result

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: The complex numbers over the reals
examples.proof: Use $\mathbf C=\mathbf R[i]\cong\mathbf R[X]/(X^2+1)$. It has real basis $1,i$, is the splitting field of the separable polynomial $X^2+1$, and is algebraically closed. It is a proper extension since $i$ is not real.
refs: Stacks 09G4 · source example or supporting result

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: A finitely generated extension of infinite degree
examples.proof: In $F(t)/F$, the element $t$ is transcendental. A nonconstant rational function $r(t)$ makes $t$ algebraic over $F(r(t))$ by cross multiplying the rational expression. Therefore $r(t)$ cannot be algebraic over $F$.
refs: Stacks 09G6 · source example or supporting result
Stacks 030X · separably generated extensions are separable

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: An algebraic extension with no finite generating set
examples.proof: Take $\overline{\mathbf F}_p/\mathbf F_p$. It is algebraic and normal, and its algebraic elements are separable because $\mathbf F_p$ is perfect. Every finite field has $q$ elements for some $q$, so $X^q-X-1$ has no root in it. An algebraically closed field is therefore infinite. Finite degree over $\mathbf F_p$ would give a finite field, and a finite algebraic generating set would give finite degree.
refs: Stacks 09GT · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09GH · finite generation in the algebraic case

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: A finite separable extension that is not normal
examples.proof: The real extension $\mathbf Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbf Q$ has degree $3$ by Eisenstein at $2$. Its defining polynomial $X^3-2$ is separable in characteristic zero and has two nonreal roots, so it does not split in the real extension.
refs: Stacks 09HM · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09G7 · degree of a simple algebraic extension

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: A finite normal extension that is not separable
examples.proof: Let $t$ be an indeterminate, $F=\mathbf F_p(t)$, and let $E=F(u)$ with $u^p=t$. The $t$-adic valuation shows that $t$ is not a $p$th power in $F$. The polynomial $X^p-t$ is irreducible, and it has only one distinct root in an algebraic closure. Each element of $E$ has its $p$th power in $F$.
refs: Stacks 09HF · source example or supporting result

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: A finite extension with no primitive element
examples.proof: Put $F=\mathbf F_p(s,t)$ and adjoin $s^{1/p}$ and $t^{1/p}$. At each step the relevant coordinate valuation shows that the coordinate is not a $p$th power. The extension has degree $p^2$. The $p$th power of every element lies in $F$, so each simple subextension has degree at most $p$. The primitive element criterion gives infinitely many intermediate fields.
refs: Stacks 030N · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09HF · adjoining a missing pth root

examples.subject: field
examples.name: A perfect field that is not algebraically closed
examples.proof: For instance take the prime field $\mathbf F_p$. In any field of $q$ elements Frobenius is bijective. The polynomial $X^q-X-1$ has no root in the field and its derivative is $-1$. An irreducible factor gives a proper separable extension.
refs: Stacks 09HY · source example or supporting result

examples.subject: field
examples.name: A positive-characteristic imperfect field
examples.proof: For $F=\mathbf F_p(t)$, the valuation of $t$ at $t=0$ is $1$. Valuations of nonzero $p$th powers are multiples of $p$, so $t$ has no $p$th root in $F$.
refs: Stacks 030Z · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09HF · irreducibility of the missing pth root polynomial

examples.subject: field
examples.name: A separably closed field that is not perfect
examples.proof: Inside an algebraic closure of $\mathbf F_p(t)$ take the subfield of all elements separable over $\mathbf F_p(t)$. It is separably closed by transitivity and the embedding theorem for algebraic closures. The root of $X^p-t$ is purely inseparable and lies outside this subfield, since that polynomial is irreducible and has one distinct root.
refs: Stacks 030K · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09GU · embedding into an algebraic closure
Stacks 09HF · irreducibility of a missing pth root

examples.subject: field-extension-pair
examples.name: Two subfields that are not linearly disjoint
examples.proof: Take $E=L=\mathbf Q(\sqrt 2)$ inside a common overfield. The elements $1,\sqrt2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbf Q$ and dependent over $L$. Equivalently $\sqrt2\otimes1-1\otimes\sqrt2$ is a nonzero tensor killed by multiplication.
refs: Stacks 09IF · source example or supporting result

examples.subject: field-extension
examples.name: An extension that cannot be generated by countably many elements
examples.proof: The field generated over $\mathbf Q$ by a countable set is countable, since every element is represented by a rational expression in finitely many generators. The complex numbers are uncountable. An algebraic extension of $\mathbf Q$ is countable by the cardinality bound.
refs: Stacks 09G0 · source example or supporting result
Stacks 09GK · cardinality bound for algebraic extensions
Stacks 09I5 · complex numbers are algebraically closed

examples.subject: ring-ideal-pair
examples.name: The localized integers: idempotents lift but the pair is not henselian
examples.proof: Take $(A,I)=(\mathbf Z_{(2)},2\mathbf Z_{(2)})$. The ideal is maximal and both the local ring and its residue field have only the idempotents zero and one. But $T^2-T+2$ reduces to the product $T(T-1)$ of comaximal monic factors, while it has no rational root, since its discriminant is $-7$. A lifted monic factorization would consist of linear factors.
refs: Stacks 09XI · idempotents in every finite algebra, rather than just the base ring

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Same topological space, different scheme
examples.proof: $\operatorname{Spec} k$ and $\operatorname{Spec}(k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2))$ each have one point; only the first is reduced. The reduction map is a universal homeomorphism.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Separated is not Hausdorff
examples.proof: The scheme $\mathbb A^1_k$ is separated over k. Its generic point lies in every nonempty open, so the Zariski space is not Hausdorff.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Quasi-affine need not be affine
examples.proof: The punctured affine plane $U=\mathbb A^2_k\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ is quasi-affine. Its global ring is $k[x,y]$, by intersecting $k[x,y]_x$ and $k[x,y]_y$ in $k(x,y)$. The canonical map to its global spectrum omits the origin and is not an isomorphism.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Quasi-separated need not be separated
examples.proof: Glue two copies of $\mathbb A^1_k$ along $D(t)$ by the identity. Their intersection is affine, and the finite affine cover makes the scheme quasi-separated. On the product of the two charts over k, the diagonal is the affine diagonal with the origin removed, so it is not closed.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Connected need not be irreducible
examples.proof: $\operatorname{Spec}(k[x,y]/(xy))$ is the union of two closed affine lines meeting at the origin. Each line is connected, hence their union is connected.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Reduced need not be normal
examples.proof: The local ring at the origin of $\operatorname{Spec}k[t^2,t^3]$ is a domain but does not contain the element t, which is integral over it. Thus the cusp is reduced and not normal.

examples.subject: morphism
examples.name: Finite type need not be finite presentation
examples.proof: Let $A=k[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$ and $I=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)$. The closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\to\operatorname{Spec} A$ is of finite type, but I is not finitely generated, so this morphism is not of finite presentation.

examples.subject: morphism
examples.name: Flat alone need not imply open
examples.proof: $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q$ → $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ is flat by localization. Its image is the generic point, which is not open.
refs: Stacks 01UA · flat morphisms locally of finite presentation are universally open

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Quasi-compact need not be quasi-separated
examples.proof: Glue two copies of Spec k[x₁,x₂,…] along the union of the principal opens D(xᵢ). The two affine charts cover the result, but their intersection is not quasi-compact: for any finite subfamily the prime generated by those variables belongs to an omitted principal open.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: Quasi-separated need not be quasi-compact
examples.proof: An infinite disjoint union of copies of Spec k is separated over Spec k: its diagonal is the union of the diagonal components in a disjoint union of point schemes. The cover by the individual copies has no finite subcover.

examples.subject: space
examples.name: A two-point spectral space that is not profinite
examples.proof: The spectrum of a discrete valuation ring has one generic point and one closed point. It is spectral, but the generic point is not closed. In the patch topology both singletons are open, so that topology is finite discrete.
refs: Stacks 08YF · spectral spaces and the constructible topology

examples.subject: space
examples.name: A compact Hausdorff space that is not profinite
examples.proof: The real interval [0,1] is compact and Hausdorff, but connected and has more than one point. It cannot be profinite, since the finite discrete coordinate quotients of a profinite space separate its points.

examples.subject: scheme
examples.name: A Noetherian space with a non-Noetherian structure sheaf
examples.proof: Let A be the square-zero extension of a field k by an infinite-dimensional k-vector space V. Every prime contains V, so Spec A consists of one point and is Noetherian as a space. The ideal V is not finitely generated over A, since the action on V factors through k.

examples.subject: space
examples.name: The p-adic integers are profinite but not extremally disconnected
examples.proof: The p-adic integers are the inverse limit of the finite discrete quotient rings modulo powers of p. The subset of nonzero elements with even p-adic valuation is open. Its closure adds 0, which is not interior because every neighbourhood of 0 also contains elements of odd valuation.
